articles.summary: The trajectory of computing costs is alarming finance chiefs already struggling to put a price tag on AI.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- No one ever wants to give a technology team a blank check. Yet for many chief financial officers, that's exactly what they were asked to do in the early rush to embrace AI. Now, after one-too-many surprise bills, finding a way to control costs has become an imperative.

It's a simmering issue in banks, where technology budgets are already under pressure from competing demands ranging from legacy IT modernization to cybersecurity. Some of the greatest hopes for productivity improvements are pinned on agentic AI, which can tackle complex tasks autonomously, but are inherently difficult to budget for as the amount of computing power each task consumes can be unpredictable.

"I actually don't think anybody in the organization has a good handle on it — if I am going to do XYZ, what is going to be my cost," said Bhavi Mehta, a partner at Bain & Co. and its global lead for advanced analytics in financial services. "As AI moves toward more sophisticated reasoning and agentic workflows, the tokens required for a given task can vary significantly. That makes understanding cost alongside business value increasingly important as banks scale AI," he added.

Only 12 of the 50 largest global banks tracked by AI benchmarking firm Evident have publicly attributed projected or realized returns to their adoption of AI, according to its latest report. Yet it's a rare CEO who doesn't talk up the potential benefits. Rising investment in the technology came up during third-quarter earnings calls at several US banks from Citigroup Inc. to Goldman Sachs Group Inc., but only a few executives had precise figures for their AI expenditures or the financial benefits they are generating.

So as the industry moves from the experimentation to the deployment stage, Bloomberg News spoke with more than a dozen engineers, executives and advisers about their experiences and strategies.

While tokenmaxxing — the practice of engineers using AI as much as possible — has become notorious — that's not always the cause of token usage blowout.

When Deutsche Bank AG's monitoring flagged individual employees consuming unusually large volumes of tokens, many turned out to be doing useful work, said Christoph Rabenseifner, the bank's chief strategy officer for technology, data and innovation. Instead of cutting them off, the bank steered that usage in a more productive direction. It also tested one task on a smaller, specially trained model instead of a large frontier model, cutting costs several times over, Rabenseifner added.

articles.title: SoftBank Market Value Poised to Halve From Peak as AI Fears Grow
articles.summary: SoftBank Group Corp.'s market value is poised to halve from its peak in June, as higher borrowing costs fuel investor concerns over the sustainability of its...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SoftBank Group Corp.'s ( SFTBY ) market value is poised to halve from its peak in June, as higher borrowing costs fuel investor concerns over the sustainability of its massive investments in artificial intelligence.

Shares of the Tokyo-based company fell as much as 6.7% on Thursday, taking their drop from an all-time high on June 2 to 50%, with earnings from US megacaps failing to ease the angst.

Global concerns over AI spending had accelerated after US-based cloud-computing provider CoreWeave Inc.'s bonds fell to levels associated with distress, exposing financing risks across the industry.

"SoftBank's vulnerability stands out as investors increasingly scrutinize the financial health of AI-related companies, given the group's highly leveraged financial structure and growing borrowing costs," said Kazuyuki Muramatsu, head of investment management at Nagomi Capital. If global sentiment toward the AI growth story turns sour, it may lead to valuation losses for SoftBank's Vision Fund, which would in turn result in higher premium for future funding, he said.

Read: CoreWeave Stock Wipeout Exposes Divide Between AI Fear and Greed

The price to insure SoftBank's debt against default has climbed, with credit-default swaps rising to the highest level in nearly four years on Tuesday. With the company relying on debt financing for much of its investments across the AI ecosystem, ranging from infrastructure and energy to robotics, CoreWeave's troubles dented confidence even in equity investors who had earlier focused on returns from SoftBank's AI bets. The stock is down more than 30% so far this month, wiping out all gains from September.

Read: SoftBank Group Credit Risk Hits 4-Year High on AI Funding Strain

Rising competition among AI models also remains an overhang. OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested almost $65 billion, now faces more affordable Chinese rivals offering comparable performance.

SoftBank raised $11.1 billion in September via the largest corporate junk bond sale on record to finance founder Masayoshi Son's big AI ambitions.

With assistance from Hideyuki Sano and Gregory Turk.

articles.title: Nokia Q3 profit rises on AI-driven network demand, outlook unchanged
articles.summary: Investing.com-- Nokia Oyj (ST:NOKIA) reported a 35% rise in third-quarter comparable operating profit on Thursday, driven by strong demand for network infras...
articles.body:
Investing.com-- Nokia Oyj ( NOK ) reported a 35% rise in third-quarter comparable operating profit on Thursday, driven by strong demand for network infrastructure used in artificial intelligence and cloud computing, while maintaining its full-year financial outlook.

The Finnish telecom equipment maker's comparable operating profit rose to 605 million euros ($680 million) in the July-September quarter from 448 million euros a year earlier.

Nokia stock fell more than 5% during premarket trading on Thursday even as sales to AI and cloud customers surged 123% in the third quarter.

Net sales increased 10% to 5.15 billion euros, while comparable operating margin expanded to 11.7% from 9.5%.

Nokia's Network Infrastructure business led growth, with sales rising 15% on a constant-currency basis, supported by a 43% increase in IP Networks and an 18% rise in Optical Networks.

Sales to AI and cloud customers surged 123%, while order intake from the segment increased 118%.

Mobile Infrastructure sales grew 5%, partly reflecting revenue brought forward from the fourth quarter, the company said.

However, reported operating profit fell 22% to 196 million euros, weighed down by restructuring and integration costs. Nokia recorded 357 million euros in restructuring-related charges during the quarter.

The company maintained its 2026 comparable operating profit forecast of 2.1 billion to 2.6 billion euros, expecting fourth-quarter sales to rise 20% to 24% sequentially.

Chief Executive Justin Hotard said Nokia expected its combined Optical and IP Networks businesses to grow 25% to 30% in 2027, supported by AI infrastructure demand.

articles.title: Claude did not invent scorpion antivenom
articles.summary: Citrini takes a stab at drug development.
articles.body: An investment research firm wanted to prove AI could revolutionize drug development. So they teamed up with Anthropic to see whether an unreleased version of Claude could make scorpion antivenom. It couldn’t. It came up with some promising starting points, but nothing close to an actual drug, experts tell The Verge. Citrini Research, the firm behind the experiment, admitted that “none of us could claim to know anything about AI as it related to biology.” That didn’t stop it from trying to make a drug from scratch — or publishing a blog post titled “We Wanted to Use Claude to Create a New Drug. Here’s What Happened.” The account came complete with rhetorical questions like “Why don’t we try to use AI to create a new drug?”, a blow-by-blow account of its amateurish scientific adventures, and a quote from Charles Darwin. If the name Citrini sounds familiar, that’s because the firm was behind a widely circulated piece of fiction imagining an AI-induced economic catastrophe that gained traction on social media and rattled real-world markets. It also claims to have visited the Strait of Hormuz in April to get a firsthand perspective on what was happening in the volatile region. For its latest venture, Citrini enlisted the help of Anthropic, which, mere weeks out from its hotly anticipated IPO, has a few reasons to talk up AI’s potential in drug development and the life sciences — two areas it’s actively pursuing. The collaboration came about after Citrini ran into Claude’s biosecurity guardrails while trying to get the model to research drug candidates. The post’s author said they “spam called anyone in my contact list who worked at an AI lab,” eventually finding a willing partner in Anthropic. The AI lab agreed to drop the restrictions and give the team access to a more advanced, unreleased model on the condition that they work from its offices. “Luckily,” Anthropic also agreed to foot the hefty compute and token bill, which came just shy of $50,000. After weighing a few options, the team settled on scorpion antivenom, a costly treatment that can be difficult to produce, often involving injecting venom into horses. The goal was to use Claude to design proteins that could bind to the toxins in scorpion venom. Armed with a 35-page prompt, they set the AI to work, unleashing some 300 subagents to discover suitable proteins. In its own more sober account of the experiment, Anthropic said Claude generated nearly 320,000 candidates, whittling them down to 180 designs after discarding those that resembled known toxins or existing proteins. The entire process took 64 hours. Anthropic said the team worked “with Claude” to add another 31 designs, bringing the total to 211. Citrini then sent the designs to two outside laboratories — Swiss biotech company Adaptyv Bio and US-based Twist Biosciences — to test whether the proteins could actually bind to their intended targets, a key step for developing an effective antivenom. That cost another $150,000, give or take. It’s unclear why Anthropic could not have conducted these tests in-house at its biology wet lab in California. Seventeen of the proteins passed muster, collectively binding to four of the five scorpion toxins the team had hoped to target. Not one of the proteins bound to more than a single toxin, Citrini said. Even if they had, Citrini would still be a very long way from a working antivenom. Binding to a toxin does not mean a protein can actually neutralize it, let alone function as a safe and effective treatment. Citrini acknowledges this itself, noting that “no experiment has yet tested whether they actually stopped the toxin working.” In other words, the experiment had not succeeded. Citrini set out to make a new drug, but experts tell The Verge it had only accomplished the relatively “easy” part of the process. “It is easy-ish to discover a good binder against snake and scorpion toxins,” said Andreas Hougaard Laustsen-Kiel, a professor of antibody technologies at the Technical University of Denmark. “The hard part is to translate it into a medicine.” Melisa Benard Valle, an assistant professor, and Anne Ljungars, a senior researcher, both at the Technical University of Denmark, agreed. “The results are technically promising, but some of the excitement is premature,” they wrote in a joint email, describing the findings as “far from a medicine and hyped.” Much remains unknown about the proteins Claude designed, they said, including their safety, stability, how they behave in the body, and whether they can be developed into viable treatments. “Translating these binders into an actual medicine is likely still a long and challenging process.” The most novel aspect of Citrini’s experiment, they said, was the “autonomous discovery process rather than the biological results.” AI has huge potential to accelerate discovery, they added, but warned “turning promising molecules into effective medicines remains a much greater challenge.” Nor is the underlying approach particularly new. Andreas Bender, a professor of machine learning in medicine at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, told The Verge existing methods like high-throughput screening “are often able to find a multitude of hits at manageable cost,” even without any AI. Designing proteins that bind to targets is “kind of” a solved problem, said Bender, who is also a visiting professor at the University of Cambridge. The much harder challenge is turning those results into treatments that actually work in living systems. “It’s exactly this translation that lacks.” While it failed to make a drug, Citrini declared the experiment a success of sorts. The firm argued it offers a glimpse into the investment opportunities emerging in the upcoming era of AI-enabled drug discovery. As for why it didn’t bother to take the research further? Citrini accused critics of “nitpick[ing]” and added, “Not to beat a dead horse, but we are an investment research firm - not a biotech startup.” Citrini and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. But it still made a bullish case for companies that might benefit. Naturally, the specifics were reserved for paying subscribers, though Bloomberg reports the firm highlighted companies involved in the testing side of drug development, including Charles River Laboratories, which supplies primates for animal research. In a video discussing the experiment, Citrini described the AI portion as “free,” conveniently overlooking the tab picked up by Anthropic. [Media:

articles.title: AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary
articles.summary: Tech companies tout AI agents that will browse, research, and shop on behalf of humans. But agents are getting blocked left and right — and even when they work, it suggests a more annoying future for humans.
articles.body: Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience. Tech companies have marketed them as personal assistants — the democratizing of labor that ordinarily would only be available to the rich and powerful. In practice, at least for buying things, it’s more like sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store: They require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications, run into technical problems regularly, and come back with solutions that are not exactly what you asked for. They did, technically speaking, complete a task, just not the specific one you asked them to, and often not in the way you would have approached it. Meta, Google, OpenAI, and others have all introduced some version of agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is. Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf. But as AI companies — and their users — are finding out, buying things requires that the other party is willing to sell them in the first place. The most prominent example of a retailer or service provider refusing to let an AI agent in has been Amazon. The retail giant sued Perplexity, with Amazon saying the AI company had ignored its requests to stop its agent from shopping on the site. More recently, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon. E-commerce sites aren’t the only platforms walling off agents: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow outside agents to access accounts, saying it was “too risky” for clients and the company, and some users report they’ve been unable to use agents to book trips from providers like Delta and Amtrak. AI agents can also get caught in the web of general bot blocking systems, meaning that even if a site doesn’t have a blanket ban, existing firewalls can make agents inconsistent — and by extension, less useful for the types of tasks tech companies tout as the future. Even without hard blocks, agents’ access to retailers is spotty. For example, Muse, which I instructed to look for a specific face moisturizer, was caught in Target’s bot check one day but was able to get through the next. It suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to my address when I searched for the best price on granola bars. When I asked for mattress recommendations under a certain price point, Muse was once again blocked by Target, despite being able to pull from the site just a few minutes prior. How successful an agent is at accessing a site may depend on how it went about the task and what safeguards are in place, Target spokesperson Loni Monroe told The Verge in an email. (Target has AI shopping partnerships with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft.) Agents may be able to access one part of the site but not another, as a way to protect customer data and the shopping experience. In addition, Monroe said that Target has safeguards preventing unauthorized agents and bots from accessing customer accounts and initiating transactions on a human’s behalf. The lack of Amazon options within agents is also impossible to ignore. Sometimes, the agents will say as much: When I asked Muse to find the best per-piece granola bar price, it offered options from Sam’s Club, Walmart, and Costco, but acknowledged a big caveat: Amazon might have had the lowest-priced option, but it was hard-blocked from browsing, so Muse couldn’t confirm. Between waiting for a response, directing Muse to search for more sites, and clarifying that a West Coast-based retailer wouldn’t ship to New York, it likely would have been faster to search myself. It also explains why agentic AI companies would really like to have Amazon on board — and why Amazon is so fiercely protective of how customers shop on its platform. It’s not that Amazon is against robots shopping in place of humans — the company has its own on-platform agentic shopping feature that monitors prices, automatically reorders items, and purchases products based on rules set by human users. Another feature that uses an agent to purchase products from other sites without leaving Amazon angered smaller businesses, who say they didn’t consent to having their storefronts scraped and featured on Amazon. Amazon spokesperson Maxine Tagay confirmed that the company “requested that Meta remove Amazon” from Muse. “We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Tagay said in an email. It’s one thing for agents to offer comically spotty, disjointed services — but it’s another, potentially more frustrating experience when they actually do work, because of the implications for humans. In order to test a shopping task that I actually would like to automate, I unleashed Muse on The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion retailer. As secondhand shopping has exploded in popularity, shopping on The RealReal has gotten increasingly competitive, so much so that the company sells a $12-per-month subscription allowing shoppers to get early access to new items. On The RealReal, part of the shopping process is zero-sum: Placing an item in your cart reserves it for you for 20 minutes, making it impossible for other people to swipe it. I instructed my Muse agent to bulk-add all 10 of the newest listings from a favorite brand to my cart, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing them before I got the chance to review the latest selections. I had no intention of buying any of these items, but I prompted Muse to keep re-adding the items to my shopping bag each time the 20-minute hold had expired. On and on this went, all day (I eventually ended the task). If I were a less honest, pure-hearted person, I would deploy an agent to run this personalized, technically allowed reserve system endlessly. But as I watched the items continuously pop back into my cart, exasperation flooded my psyche — on behalf of the other shoppers interested in these items, but also for my future self, who may soon be competing with someone else’s agent doing this same thing. Perhaps I already am. The RealReal sees AI agents as an opportunity, and is investing in its own AI-powered services while protecting the integrity of the platform, chief technology officer Luke Friang told The Verge in an email. “Our approach is to remain open to third-party AI agents, allowing them to browse, log in and interact with our marketplace, while maintaining safeguards against automated activity that could disrupt the customer experience,” Friang said. To be sure, normal online shopping can be tedious, too — the endless array of options on the web can make finding the right thing feel like looking for a needle in a haystack. Agentic shopping is the inverse: It’s like looking at the world through a pinhole. If I don’t like the five options Muse has curated for me, I must ask it to find five more, and on and on. I must give the agent specific parameters and rules, and expand and tweak them as needed, little by little. A more rote task like finding the absolute lowest price on a product you already know you want is where an agent could be truly useful. Without Amazon, though, even that feels like the task was carried out with incomplete information. If you have preferences about literally anything you spend money on — the price, the return policy, the shipping rates, the ethical standards of a company, the fabric composition — an agent is just another entity to express those preferences to. With the time and patience for hand-holding, Muse could help deepen a search for something specific: For example, I uploaded photos to Muse of a vintage dress I’ve been hunting for, along with the specific year it’s from, a list of keywords associated with it, notes about similar items, and secondhand platforms to start searches on. Muse could not find the dress for sale anywhere, but it did alert me to an upcoming auction of items from the same brand. In an email, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton emphasized the partnerships the company has forged with retailers and the control human users have over the agent’s actions. “Importantly, users can take over at any time, Muse is designed to always ask permission before buying, and it applies ethical browsing principles when asked to do things that a human could not - like buying all the tickets to an event,” Clayton said. “The response from retailers has been overwhelmingly positive, and we look forward to working with them as we continue to grow Muse and improve the purchasing experience.” There’s another thing that nags at me no matter how long I tinker with agentic shopping: The joy and thrill of discovery is largely gone. Buying things is an American pastime. We do it in person, online, from strangers on Facebook, and from professional salespeople on livestreams. We buy things we need and we buy things we don’t, things we know we want and the things we’ve never seen until now that have suddenly become very important. It’s not a stretch to say that for many, shopping is a hobby — one that has become solidly entangled with another, more modern hobby of scrolling on a phone. We don’t just lust after material belongings; we imbue them with identity markers and social status. Buying things is intensive — in resources, in labor, in emotion. AI companies see this pastime as something that can be optimized. Many people would probably prefer that it not be.

articles.title: What’s the PHP coding flaw that could pull down 70 percent of the internet?
articles.summary: The vulnerability allows a hacker to change a website or extract data, including personal information.
articles.body:
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere have gone offline after news of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems.

Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately”.

PHP runs on the servers that host websites, building pages behind the scenes before they reach a visitor’s browser. Most people never see it, but it powers everything from blogs to online shops and government portals.

The vulnerabilities, which had been lurking in the software for years, were uncovered with the help of artificial intelligence. Details about them leaked online on Tuesday before fixes were available, forcing PHP to rush them out.

Experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.

Andrew Cullen, a lecturer on AI and cybersecurity at the University of Melbourne, said many devices in the world are connected to one piece of foundational software, which is where the bug was found.

The vulnerability allows a hacker to run code on a website, meaning they could change the website or force it to release personal information collected in a database, Cullen told Al Jazeera.

Both flaws stem from how PHP handles fatal errors, such as running out of memory. Because the problem sits in PHP itself, even the simplest website running an affected version can be vulnerable, and attackers could read passwords and other credentials from a server’s memory, the cloud security company Wiz said. Both flaws scored 9.2 out of 10 on the industry’s standard severity scale, placing them in the “critical” category.

The two flaws, nicknamed PHP2Shell, were found independently by two cybersecurity companies using AI. Calif, working with OpenAI, reported the first on August 11. Wiz, which is owned by Google, reported the second on August 24.

The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz said in a statement.

Calif and Wiz said they had coordinated with each other, the PHP team and OpenAI before making the vulnerabilities public.

However, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said his security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities on October 17, four days before the public disclosure.

Moses said it was unclear how the hacker learned of the flaws while Calif’s and Wiz’s reports were still under embargo. Security researchers usually keep details of flaws secret until a fix is ready, so attackers cannot use them in the meantime.

PHP, a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for Personal Home Page, underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences.

Calif, Wiz and the web infrastructure company Cloudflare said the flaws affect PHP 5.4 and later versions, more than a decade of releases.

Cullen said the vulnerability was “really unprecedented”, noting that PHP powers more than 70 percent of websites globally, although sites that have been updated are protected.

“There is a real risk to the kind of shared digital infrastructure that we all rely on,” Cullen told Al Jazeera. “There is concern in the cybersecurity community about what the blast radius for this will be, even though the developers of PHP have been very quick to try and develop patches for it.”

Cullen added that while AI was getting better at cybersecurity, it was also getting better at being a hacker. “This means that we are developing systems … that are making the internet safer by helping to fix bugs, but we’re also making it riskier by discovering bugs and creating bugs they’ll be able to hack,” he said.

In the Netherlands, the Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. Several organisations followed the example and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites for the country’s five largest political parties and several hospital ‌websites.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he was closely monitoring the situation.

Disruptions were even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline “as a precautionary measure”.

France’s Ministry of the Interior said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance.

Belgium’s Federal Public Service Foreign Affairs, Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation said it had temporarily taken its websites offline after reports of cyberattacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities although the country’s cybersecurity centre said it had not recorded any attacks on Belgian websites.

South Korea’s ⁠government raised ⁠its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures. It issued security guidance to about 28,000 companies with registered chief information security officers and 5,900 members ⁠of a government information-sharing ⁠network as well as operators of critical infrastructure, web-hosting firms and data centres.

The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue.

articles.title: 1Password lets AI agents use your passwords without seeing them
articles.summary: 1Password is introducing a new feature that allows AI agents to sign into your accounts without actually seeing or handling your passwords.
articles.body: 1Password is introducing a new feature that allows AI agents to sign into your accounts without actually seeing or handling your passwords. The aptly named 1Password for Agents doesn’t give bots free reign to access all of your connected accounts — you’ll still need to grant approval for sign-in requests — but should make it less cumbersome to use Agents for tasks that require them to log into various services. ”Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf. The old model where you hand over a credential and hope for the best doesn’t work,” 1Password chief product officer Aashish Tripathi said in a press statement. “An agent should be able to do the job it’s been asked to do without getting permanent access to everything behind the account, and 1Password provides the trust layer that makes this possible across personal agent experiences.” With this new system, an AI agent uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password when it reaches a sign-in form. The app then sends you a notification about which account credentials it needs, and why. If you choose to approve the request, 1Password will fill in the required login information instead of handing it to the agent. Approvals are granted on your own device to ensure you’re behind the permissions, making this a similar process to two-factor authentication. After the agent is signed in, it’ll continue with its task, without ever having actually seen your password. [Media: This 1Password access system is designed to work with a variety of popular AI agents, including Meta Muse, ChatGPT Work and Dots, Claude Duet, Grok Bot, and Town. 1Password says more partners are working to bring support to 1Password for Agents, including Browserbase, Browser Use, Dana, Instinct, Kernel, Perplexity, Ramp, Tomo, and Wajo, with “additional integrations to come.” Correction, October 22nd: Aashish Tripathi is 1Password’s chief product officer, not CEO.

articles.title: Nirva raises $33M for a pendant that only listens to you
articles.summary: Nirva will ship its $249 ambient AI pendant by the end of the year.
articles.body:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon launched a new wrist-worn device with Bee; a former Plaud exec launched ambient apps through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple launched Voice Intelligence features during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called Nirva is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.

The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.

Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.

The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.

Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.

In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.

“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.

For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.

Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.

In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.

Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.

“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.

The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.

Lyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.

The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.

Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.

The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’ Taya , which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

articles.title: Claude Duet app is Anthropic’s bet on agents
articles.summary: Claude Duet is available through waitlist for Pro and Max plan users.
articles.body:
The AI world is flooded with personal and productivity-based assistants , with new ones launching every week. Now, Anthropic is entering this battle in the hopes of gaining user attention with a new app called Claude Duet, aimed at rivaling Meta Muse , OpenAI Dots , Hark , Instinct , Grok Bot , and Fo .

Anthropic said the new agent is meant to cater to professionals and small businesses to help them with automating and managing tasks. The company is making a distinction from personal agents such as Instinct , by noting that Duet isn’t good at handling errands or booking tickets, and it can’t show you its browser use as it happens.

Instead, Duet can build a daily briefing for its users, create dashboards, or suggest actions based on the user’s data. Like other agents, Duet can complete tasks in the background through its own virtual machine while you handle other things, then come back to you if it needs your approval.

The launch arrives as the market shifts beyond AI assistants to agents that can work on users’ behalf. Many of Anthropic’s rivals are focusing on business use cases. While Meta’s Muse is a personal AI assistant, the company also released a version to cater to small businesses with connections to other apps . OpenAI’s Dots has a business slant as well, with its integration with professional tools .

Anthropic says Duet proactively delivers its recommendations as it monitors ongoing tasks. Built on the Claude Opus 5.5 model, Duet can connect to over 6,000 connectors and plug-ins in the Claude Marketplace. It can also make online purchases on users’ behalf via Stripe’s ⁠Link digital wallet or Shopify’s Shop Pay.

The company said sensitive steps like payments would require user approval. However, Duet won’t trade securities or move money between accounts.

Anthropic also released a new classifier to check each message to prevent sensitive information from leaking out. It said that, by default, the agent would turn down requests asking for credit card numbers and government identification.

Claude Duet is available as an app on iOS and Android, and on the web through Claude.ai for Pro and Max customers in research preview. Users have to join a waitlist to try it.

articles.title: AI Agents Are Accessing U.S. Bank Accounts Without Their Approval. Lenders Are Pushing Back.
articles.summary: Some automated assistants appear to be taking actions beyond users' instructions, prompting questions about account security and who bears responsibility whe...
articles.body:
Major U.S. banks are detecting third-party artificial intelligence agents accessing customer accounts without bank authorization, with some automated tools appearing to act independently of their users' instructions, according to a new report.

Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are among the institutions responding to the activity, which has raised concerns about customer security and the ability of banks to monitor increasingly sophisticated software.

The Axios investigation cited people familiar with the matter who said some banks were aware of unauthorized access involving AI agents. In certain cases, the tools contacted bank call centers or appeared to perform tasks that customers had not specifically requested.

The reported incidents do not necessarily involve hackers breaking into accounts. Some customers voluntarily provide their login credentials to AI assistants designed to manage financial information or complete tasks on their behalf. However, using those credentials to access banking systems can violate institutional policies, even when the customer has granted permission.

Banks are struggling to distinguish between legitimate customer activity, authorized software and agents operating outside their intended instructions, the report said.

JPMorgan Chief Executive Jamie Dimon addressed the issue during the bank's latest earnings call last week, warning that financial institutions needed safeguards against outside AI tools that could compromise customer information or financial assets.

Dimon said the bank was not opposed to using AI agents and was already deploying the technology internally. However, it would not allow unrestricted access by outside providers.

"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company," Dimon said, explaining that the risks were too significant for customers and the bank.

In the JPMorganChase third-quarter earnings transcript, Dimon also raised concerns about liability when customers rely on AI tools that subsequently misuse their information.

Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum provided further details about the bank's approach. He said some outside financial services obtain access through credential sharing or screen scraping, a process in which software retrieves information directly from a customer's online banking interface.

JPMorgan considers those methods insecure and is blocking them where possible, Barnum said. He cautioned that customers could face consequences if they gave their credentials to an agent that subsequently carried out an unwanted transaction.

articles.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
articles.body:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.

Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.

That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.

“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.

Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”

Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.

OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

articles.title: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
articles.summary: In new research, Microsoft’s AI tool diagnosed medical cases up to four times more accurately than human physicians.
articles.body: For years, AI leaders have touted healthcare as one of the clearest examples of where their technology will improve lives. Now “it is finally here,” Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge. The company claims to have developed an AI-powered tool it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. The findings, published Thursday in one of the world’s most prestigious journals, Science, are based on tests pitting Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark, SDBench, which it plans to open-source. Designed to function like a panel of medical experts, Microsoft’s Diagnostic Orchestrator uses multiple AI agents to reason through symptoms and medical histories, decide what tests to order, and arrive at a diagnosis, mimicking the process doctors use to investigate cases. On cases taken from hundreds of reports published in The New England Journal of Medicine, Microsoft’s system achieved a diagnostic accuracy of around 83 percent, compared with roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians using references and 22 percent for those working without them. The Diagnostic Orchestrator also outperformed doctors on emergency department cases drawn from a large database of patient admissions at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, scoring 80 percent accuracy compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. The AI system also tended to reach its diagnoses at a lower estimated cost than human counterparts. The researchers say that the system, which is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5, also outperformed frontier AI models operating on their own, though the peer-reviewed paper does not include newer models like GPT-6 Astra, Meta’s Muse Wonder Full, Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, or Anthropic’s Opus 5.5. The Diagnostic Orchestrator was first developed when GPT-4.1 was the most advanced model available, but the researchers say subsequent testing suggests that “improvements in model capability do not necessarily diminish the benefits” of having multiple agents work together. Microsoft acknowledges there’s a long road ahead before the technology can be widely deployed. While the tests more closely mirror the way doctors diagnose conditions — asking questions, weighing possible explanations, and ordering tests before reaching a diagnosis — the system has only been tested on past medical cases and it remains unclear how well it would perform in real clinical settings. “It needs clinical validation,” Suleyman says. “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.” The research is part of a broader ambition at Microsoft to develop what the company calls “medical superintelligence” — AI that can outperform the best human-led healthcare systems. Microsoft has used the term “superintelligence” since before Donald Trump and his administration co-opted it as a catch-all replacement for “AI.” Diagnosis is just part of Microsoft’s health vision, says the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, a coauthor of the study. In a blog post published Thursday and a forthcoming article in the BMJ Digital Health & AI medical journal, the company outlines five other areas it believes AI will need to master, including coordinating clinical care, making treatment decisions, and handling the human side of medicine. King tells The Verge that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system in hospital settings with the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to see how it performs in real-world clinical environments. Neither King nor Suleyman would commit to a firm timeline, though King says it will likely “get underway in the next couple of months.” Commercialization could also be on the horizon, though Microsoft has yet to say when or how the technology might become available. The company already has a significant presence in US healthcare through its digital tools, and health is one of the most popular uses for its consumer-facing chatbot Copilot. King emphasizes the need for a responsible rollout, noting the high regulatory and compliance requirements in medicine that would need to be followed. “Next year we’re going to see extremely impressive deployments of intelligent systems in production,” Suleyman says. “I think that this is just going to change the way care is delivered in a big way.” Suleyman has spoken previously about his “human-centered” vision for AI, and said medicine is no exception. Even as he predicts the arrival of “something that is indistinguishable from human performance on medical superintelligence in the next couple of years,” he insists that human clinicians should and will always have a central role in patient care. While he acknowledges AI could end up with doctors being handed more work, he says his hope is that it will take some of “the drudgery” out of medicine, freeing up clinicians to spend more time with patients. “I’m very optimistic about what’s coming next,” he says. “I think this is why we build technology.”

articles.title: In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse
articles.summary: “Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call.
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?” Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.” The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said during the call, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which, as of today, bring in pretty much all the money Meta makes. This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.” Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years. All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned in to Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one. To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by more than 10 million users in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce: A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending, on average, more than $200 per purchase. Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time. Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a YouTuber said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been reports of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told Bloomberg earlier this week that it would consider blocking Muse from accessing its customers’ financial data. Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending, Supermarket Sweep episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New research from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up. If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care. “Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s CFO Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees. Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday, it owes New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it. Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency. It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already research on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy-use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it. Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself. “One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base. Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said, adding, “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.” Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.” Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
articles.body:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”

The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.

In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.

“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”

In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.

The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.

Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.

Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.

With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.

DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.

Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.

Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.

“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”

Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.

“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.

He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”

“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”

Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.

“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.

He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.

Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.

“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”

Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes.

“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs.

Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.

“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

articles.title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI is launching its decision model to the world. Can it compete with the original Jev?
articles.body:
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company .

TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.

Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.

“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”

Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.

In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.

Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.

Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.

The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”

Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.

Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”

As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

articles.title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts.
articles.body:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.

Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.

The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.

1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.

“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”

Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.

This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.

Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

articles.title: Anthropic IPO to Drive Blockbuster Gains for Iconiq, Spark, GIC
articles.summary: By the time Iconiq made its first investment in Anthropic PBC in 2025, the artificial intelligence developer was valued at $183 billion — more than almost an...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- By the time Iconiq made its first investment in Anthropic PBC in 2025, the artificial intelligence developer was valued at $183 billion — more than almost any other tech startup in the world — and well on its way to becoming an AI juggernaut. Yet even Iconiq's later stage bet is now set to bring in massive returns as Anthropic nears its Wall Street debut.The investment firm, which has pumped more than $6 billion into Anthropic, owns a stake worth approximately $17 billion based on the AI company's most recent $965 billion private market valuation, according to people familiar with the matter. The value of Iconiq's investment — the largest deal in its history — could double if Anthropic pulls off its public offering at a valuation as high as $2 trillion, as some expect. Anthropic's imminent public listing is poised to create multibillion-dollar gains for top venture capital firms, technology companies and independent investors that have backed the Claude chatbot maker since its founding in 2021. The list of winners includes prescient early backers as well as comparative latecomers who benefitted from the company's rapid ascent and surging valuation over the past year.Spark Capital, the only venture firm known to have a board director seat at the startup, invested $75 million in Anthropic in 2023, one person said, marking its largest check ever. Its stake is now worth $7 billion at the current valuation, the person said. Sound Ventures, an under-the-radar firm started by talent manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in that same round at a $5 billion valuation, another person said. It has since invested $400 million across subsequent financings, leading to a stake worth billions of dollars, the person said. The firm is now run by Oseary and Effie Epstein, managing partner. Kutcher stepped down earlier this year.

By contrast, Sequoia Capital, the storied venture firm that made early bets on OpenAI, only cut its first check to Anthropic at the start of this year. But the $3 billion it's put into the startup has given Sequoia a roughly 1% stake, according to a person familiar with the matter, setting it up for a significant return. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC also owns about 1% of Anthropic after investing north of $4.5 billion in the company, starting with its first investment last year, said one person, who like others spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. In August, Anthropic formed a strategic partnership with GIC and Macquarie Asset Management to build data centers.Anthropic, Sequoia, Iconiq, Sound and GIC declined to comment. Spark did not respond to a request for comment. The Wall Street Journal previously reported some details of Spark's returns. Anthropic is expected to publicly file IPO paperwork in the coming days, kicking off the process for a public offering that could serve as an almost unparalleled wealth creation event — bolstering the net worth of its seven billionaire co-founders and turning many of the company's thousands of employees into millionaires. The IPO windfall will also likely reverberate throughout the tech and venture ecosystem, helping to fuel future investments in AI at a moment of heightened concerns about a possible bubble.Like archrival OpenAI, Anthropic has tapped numerous sources for capital to fund its costly investments in chips, data centers and talent to build better AI models and support growing adoption of its technology. Some of Anthropic's biggest suppliers, including Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Amazon.com Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have invested billions in the startup. Those deals, which elicited concerns about circular financing arrangements propping up the AI boom, are set to generate substantial returns for the big tech firms.In its early days, however, Anthropic mostly received backing from wealthy angel investors, such as former Google chief executive officer Eric Schmidt and disgraced FTX co-founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Schmidt owns around a 1% stake in the company, Bloomberg News has reported, setting him up for one of the largest gains of any individual shareholder.

articles.title: Meta turns Muse sharing back on
articles.summary: Meta has re-enabled the ability to share your conversations with Muse after security researchers reported that the public links to the conversations could be easy to find.
articles.body: Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company’s internal revenue review and a small business owner’s loan application. Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation’s title and written into public DNS. Ars Technica said Tuesday that Meta paused the sharing feature after it reached out about what was going on. In a post today on X, Meta’s David Singleton says that “The underlying issue is now fixed, and sharing is back on.” According to Singleton, the issue was with URLs for shared Muse artifacts, which Meta says are things like documents and images inside Muse, and wasn’t a flaw with chat sharing. “If you shared an artifact before the fix: it now has a new URL,” Singleton says. “Anyone visiting the old link will see a note asking them to get the new one from you. We know that’s a pain, and we’re sorry for the disruption — but protecting user data has to come first.”

articles.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
articles.summary: Meta updated its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on sites that use its platform, but legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this doesn’t address their concerns.
articles.body: Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab. Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl. Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab. Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”
